passage: Gargi, you look tired after the trip to your parents' house, so let me tell you about mine. At twenty-five, every visit home left me sour for days. My father had always compared me with my elder cousin and beaten me down with words whenever my marks slipped. The moment I walked into the flat, I turned twelve again and snapped at everything. One night, on the balcony, I said aloud, "It was unfair, and it still hurts." That was the first time I stopped arguing with the memory. I decided to visit for two days, not five, to leave the old topics alone, and I saw a counsellor. I never announced that my father was forgiven, and I never made him pay. I just stopped acting as if nothing had happened. Harsha

qa.q: How long did Harsha decide each visit should last?
qa.a: Harsha decided on two days instead of five.

qa.q: Why did saying it aloud on the balcony matter to Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha felt relief at admitting the hurt was real, and so stopped arguing with the memory.

qa.q: What steps did Harsha take to manage the visits home?
qa.a: Shorter visits, leaving the old topics alone, and seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had chosen to punish the father forever?
qa.a: The resentment would stay in charge of Harsha's life instead of being acknowledged and managed.

grounding: An elder recalls carrying pain from an unfair childhood that flared on visits home, acknowledging it, choosing limits and seeing a counsellor.
